Hatchlings of Dermochelys coriacea emerge from their nests after an incubation period of approximately 63 days [ab = approximately 63 days] at a mean nest temperature of 29.88 °C [T = 29.88 °C], a duration that aligns with typical values for tropical nesting sites. Upon emergence, straight carapace length (SCL) averages 6.18 cm [Lb = 6.18 cm], with neonates exhibiting a wet weight at birth of 46.03 grams [Wwb = 46.03 grams] and a corresponding dry weight at birth of 9.776 grams . These initial dimensions reflect the substantial yolk reserves allocated by the gravid female, whose eggs possess an initial wet weight of 83.59 grams [Ww0 = 83.59 grams] at oviposition. The transition from yolk-dependent embryo to free-swimming juvenile is marked by the completion of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical trophic switch that begins shortly after the hatchling reaches the ocean surface. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the relatively large size of leatherback hatchlings provides a survival advantage during the high-mortality dispersal phase.

After departing the nesting beach, juvenile leatherbacks embark on a prolonged growth phase that spans decades before their first successful breeding event. Field studies employing skeletochronology on humerus ossicles have established that the mean time to first reproduction for Northwest Atlantic stock is 19.25 years after hatching [tR = 19.25 years after hatching], a value recorded in environments with an average water temperature of 21.13 °C [T = 21.13 °C]. This delayed reproductive schedule is accompanied by the achievement of a specific body size; the straight carapace length at puberty using standard conversion methods is 125.6 cm [Lp = 125.6 cm], which corresponds closely to values reported by Avens and colleagues for nesting females. During this extended juvenile period, individuals traverse vast oceanic distances and undergo a substantial increase in somatic mass, reflecting the considerable time required to accumulate the energy reserves necessary for a successful first breeding season. The progression from hatchling to reproductively viable organism is therefore a slow and energetically demanding process that shapes the species' overall life history strategy.

Physiological investigations of resting metabolism in adult leatherbacks at a body temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have documented a mass-specific metabolic rate of 0.41 watts per kilogram . This figure is notably low compared to other marine reptiles of comparable size, highlighting the energetic efficiency of these gelatinous-prey specialists. The maximum intake of jellyfish by a fully grown individual, measured under field conditions at the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], is estimated at 1.13 watts per kilogram , a value derived from energy budget calculations incorporating prey energy density and observed feeding rates. Such a high maximum feeding rate relative to basal metabolism underscores the need for intensive foraging bouts to support both basal maintenance requirements and the substantial energetic demands of reproduction, particularly during the remigration interval when females must replenish depleted lipid stores before the next nesting season.

Female leatherbacks nesting on beaches of the Northwest Atlantic stock exhibit a well-characterized reproductive output. The ultimate wet weight of a reproductively active adult female averages 370 kilograms [Wwi = 370 kilograms], though historic records indicate that exceptionally large individuals can exceed 600 kilograms, reflecting the species' capacity for considerable intraspecific variation in asymptotic body mass, a pattern also seen in other large-bodied sea turtles such as the loggerhead. Nesting females produce an average of 5 clutches per nesting season [F_R_i = 5 clutches per nesting season], with each clutch containing roughly 82 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing roughly 82 eggs]. The combination of moderate clutch frequency and large clutch size yields a substantial annual reproductive effort, although the ultimate reproduction rate is tempered by a remigration interval of approximately 2.7 years between successive nesting seasons, resulting in an effective annual frequency of about 1.85 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 1.85 clutches per year]. This protracted breeding cycle contributes to the species' overall slow pace of life and low population resilience.

Estimates of maximum lifespan in the wild for Dermochelys coriacea indicate that individuals can persist for a total of 30.25 years [am = 30.25 years] under the thermal conditions typical of the Northwest Atlantic (mean water temperature of 21.13 °C [T = 21.13 °C]), a value that integrates the 19.25 years to first reproduction followed by approximately 11 years of post-maturation survival. This longevity, which places leatherbacks among the longer-lived members of the family Dermochelyidae, is achieved despite the constant energetic challenges of a pelagic existence and the physiological demands of long-distance migration between high-latitude foraging grounds and low-latitude nesting beaches. The ultimate straight carapace length attained by nesting females, averaged across multiple studies, is 151.07 cm [Li = 151.07 cm], although some model-based estimates from earlier work suggest values around 140 cm [Li = 140 cm]. Such size variation may reflect differences in foraging success across ocean basins, highlighting the ecological flexibility that has enabled leatherbacks to persist as the largest extant turtle species throughout their global distribution.
